claims.reason: Passage 4 states Jack Lindsey leads Anthropic's "model psychiatry" team and concludes models show a limited, functional form of introspective awareness that is highly limited and context-dependent.

Passage 5 confirms Chris Olah and Josh Batson work on circuit-tracing research that found the "can't answer" default pathway and their publications are the main source for mechanistic explanations of hallucination.
Passage 6 states Sam Marks has worked on how models represent truth internally (the "geometry of truth" line of work) and on auditing models for hidden objectives.
Passage 8 identifies Sebastian Farquhar and Yarin Gal as lead authors of the 2024 Nature paper on semantic entropy, the best-known method for detecting confabulations by sampling multiple answers.

Passage 9 states Adam Tauman Kalai is lead author of the 2025 paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate," which argues that training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, essential for understanding the incentive problem.
Passage 10 describes Owain Evans' influential work on whether models know what they know, including teaching models to express uncertainty in words and describing their learned behaviors.
Passage 12 states Stephen Fleming is a leading neuroscientist of human metacognition who applies metacognition research to AI, clarifying the calibration-versus-discrimination distinction.
Passage 14 confirms Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor wrote an agent reliability paper borrowing methods from nuclear and aviation safety and produce a skeptical, data-driven newsletter.
Passage 15 states METR measures how long agents can complete tasks autonomously and their reports are a key reference for reliability-over-horizon assessments.
Passage 16 states Andrej Karpathy popularized the "march of nines" framing and writes clearly about moving from demos to products.
Passage 17 states Azalia Mirhoseini co-led the LLM-as-a-Verifier work on scaling verification as its own axis.

Passage 19 states Shreya Shankar researches LLM pipeline evaluation, including the paper "Who Validates the Validators?" on aligning automated judges with human judgment to address verifier reliability.
Passage 20 describes Hamel Husain as a practical voice on building evals for real products, emphasizing error analysis, reading traces, and designing checks that catch real failures.
Passage 21 states Eugene Yan writes accessible, practical pieces on LLM evaluation and production patterns.

Passage 23 recommends a minimal follow set: Anthropic's interpretability publications, Princeton newsletter, METR, Husain and Shankar for engineering practice, and arXiv searches for "metacognition," "calibration," "selective prediction," and "process verifier".

omitted_concepts.description: Affiliations change often in this field, so it's worth checking researchers' latest pages.
Yarin Gal leads the OATML group at Oxford.
Owain Evans leads the research nonprofit Truthful AI.
Stephen Fleming authored the book "Know Thyself."
Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor are affiliated with Princeton.
METR was founded by Beth Barnes.
Azalia Mirhoseini is affiliated with Stanford.
Shreya Shankar is affiliated with UC Berkeley.
Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar teach together and their writing pairs well.
The minimal set covers the full chain from why models don't know when they're wrong to building systems that catch it; newest papers appeared in just the past few months.

review.summary: All 15 claims are fully supported by their cited passages. Each claim accurately reflects the source's descriptions of researchers, their work, and the recommended follow set. No claims are duplicated, misattributed, or lack atomicity. The omitted concepts capture notable affiliations, organizational roles, and contextual caveats not included in the claims but present in the source.
